readerTitle: Two wholesalers, one road: why the narrower promise won
caseNote: 가상 사례 (전기자재 도매상 두 곳, 사내 데이터 분석팀) + 실제 기업 광고 문구 (FedEx)
insight: 브랜드 약속은 마케팅 문구가 아니라 고객이 확인할 수 있는 운영상의 약속이며, 무엇을 하지 않을지까지 정해 준다.
misconception: 브랜드 약속은 마케팅팀이 정하는 멋진 슬로건이고, 좋은 점을 많이 약속할수록 브랜드가 강해진다.

sources.text: FedEx company history and advertising archive ("When it absolutely, positively has to be there overnight")
도매상과 사내 분석팀 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: FedEx 문구 "When it absolutely, positively has to be there overnight"는 1978년경 시작된 광고 캠페인으로 알려져 있습니다. 정확한 문구와 사용 시기를 FedEx 공식 자료로 확인하세요. 카드에는 연도를 적지 않았습니다.
도매상 두 곳과 분석팀 사례, '3시 주문·7시 도착' 같은 조건은 모두 가상입니다. 실제 성과 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Two wholesalers, one road: why the narrower promise won
body: Two electrical supply wholesalers sit on the same road. Similar prices, similar stock, similar staff.
The first one's sign says: *Quality. Service. Value.* The second one's says: *Order by 3 pm. On your job site by 7 am.*
A few years later, most local electricians call the second one first. The difference is not the products. It's what each one promised.

image.label: Two wholesaler storefronts with different signs
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 같은 길에 나란히 선 전기자재 도매상 두 곳. 왼쪽 간판 "Quality. Service. Value.", 오른쪽 간판 "Order by 3 pm. On site by 7 am." 오른쪽 가게 앞에만 작업복 차림 전기기사들이 줄 서 있음. 실제 로고·상표 사용 금지.

cards.title: You run the first wholesaler.
body: Sales are flat. Contractors say you're "fine" but rarely think of you first. You want to sharpen what your business stands for.
What do you do?

options.text: Add to the list: Quality. Service. Value. Expertise.
options.feedback: It covers more ground, but every rival claims the same words. A longer list gives customers nothing new to count on.

options.text: Pick one thing contractors need and can check, and promise it only if you can deliver it every time
options.feedback: You give up sounding good at everything. In return, customers know exactly why to call you, and each order proves it.

options.text: Hire an agency for a bolder logo and tagline
options.feedback: Fresh design can get noticed. But if the tagline promises nothing specific, contractors' experience stays the same, and so does their opinion.

cards.title: One promise could be checked. The other couldn't.
body: For an electrician, a crew waiting for parts is money burning. The second wholesaler named that exact pain and promised to remove it.
Better still, contractors could test it. A van either arrived by 7 am or it didn't. Every on-time delivery became proof.
*Quality, service, value* sounds nice, but nobody can check it on a Tuesday morning. So it earned no credit, even when the first wholesaler did good work.

cards.title: The brand promise
body: A **brand promise** is the specific thing customers can count on from you, every time they deal with you.
It's not the slogan. The slogan is how you *say* it. The promise is what you *do*.
A strong promise passes three tests: it's specific enough to check, it matters to the customer, and you can keep it on your worst day, not just your best.

image.label: Three checks: specific, matters, keepable
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 가운데 큰 약속 카드 "On site by 7 am". 주위에 체크 표시 세 개 "Specific enough to check", "Matters to the customer", "Keepable on a bad day". 옆에 흐릿한 "Quality. Service. Value." 카드는 체크가 비어 있음.

cards.title: A promise runs the business, not just the ads.
body: To keep "on site by 7 am," the second wholesaler had to change how it worked:
list: A night shift that picks orders after the 3 pm cutoff
Its own vans instead of shared couriers
Deep stock of the most-used parts, thinner stock of rare ones
Not always the lowest price, because speed costs money
cards.callout: A real promise tells you what to say no to.
cards.softwareNote: For a software product, the promise might be "set up in one afternoon, no IT team needed." Keeping it shapes the roadmap: features that add setup steps get cut or hidden, even if a few big customers ask for them.

cards.title: A promise you could check against a clock.
body: FedEx built its early reputation on a line that was really a promise: *When it absolutely, positively has to be there overnight.*
Customers didn't have to trust adjectives. They could look at the delivery time. The line worked because the planes, sorting hubs and couriers were built to keep it.
The same idea applies inside companies. Internal teams have brands too. Colleagues decide whether to bring you work based on what they believe you'll reliably do.

image.label: A package and a clock showing early morning
image.brief: 아침 시계(오전 시간)를 배경으로 문 앞에 놓인 소포 상자. 상자에 체크 표시. 실제 택배사 로고와 색상 사용 금지.

cards.title: A broken promise costs more than a vague one.
body: A specific promise makes every miss visible. If the 7 am van shows up at 10 once a week, contractors remember the misses, not the slogan.
So check how often you keep it today before you announce it. If operations can't deliver yet, fix operations first.
And keeping it has a price: extra staff, stock or capacity. Make sure customers value the promise enough to cover that cost.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a company.
body: You lead the data analysis team in a 2,000-person company. Other teams see you as a black hole: requests go in, and nobody knows when anything comes out.
Which promise should your team make?

options.feedback: It sounds generous, but it invites even more requests you can't handle. The black-hole reputation gets worse, not better.

options.text: "A clear yes, no or delivery date on every request within one working day"
options.feedback: It doesn't promise speed on every project, which you can't control. It promises an answer, which you can, and colleagues can check it.
These are the right qualities, but nobody can test them. Colleagues will judge you on the same delays as before.

cards.title: Promise one thing customers can check, then build the business to keep it.
body: A brand promise is earned in operations, one kept promise at a time. Words only point to it.
**Try it today:** finish this sentence: "Customers can always count on us to…" If a customer couldn't check your answer, make it more specific.
